evidence_set: The review reports ketamine as a non-competitive open-channel blocker at the phencyclidine site inside the NMDA receptor channel, with a trapping capability of about 86%, against more than 98% for phencyclidine and 100% for MK-801. Reported affinities for racemic ketamine in the presence of magnesium span Ki 0.18 to 3.1 micromolar across about twenty studies, including human cortex values of 0.42 (SE 0.03) and 0.67 (SE 0.15) micromolar; which subunits are blocked most depends on the magnesium present, and one cited study found no subunit difference. The tabulated values come mostly from rodent tissue, with dog and guinea pig brain as well, and from recombinant receptors in cell lines and oocytes, with two human cortex samples; the review describes brain tissue as post-mortem only for the separate Oye et al. (1992) enantiomer measurements.
III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Table 3, NMDAR rows

A 40-minute intravenous infusion of 0.5 mg/kg, the regimen used in antidepressant studies, was estimated to produce a maximum NMDA receptor occupancy of 31% plus or minus 18%, close to the 32% plus or minus 6% estimated for an antidepressant-relevant dose in rats (10 mg/kg intraperitoneally); the review does not say whether these spreads are standard deviations or standard errors. The occupancy figures are estimates taken from a cited study (Shaffer et al., 2014), not measurements made in this review.
III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 3rd paragraph (the first running paragraph after Table 3)
III. Pharmacodynamics > A. N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptors, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Table 3, norKET, DHNK and HNK rows

The review's working test is whether a target is affected within the concentrations reached in people, which by its own Table 1 are about 0.8 micromolar after the antidepressant infusion and about 5 to 10 micromolar at anaesthesia. Most other targets fall outside that range, at about 10 to 1000 micromolar: opioid receptors in the tens to hundreds, sigma receptors 19 to 139 in the text (Table 3 also lists a racemic Ki of 0.15), the serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine transporters from about 4.6 to 290, most above 60, sodium and calcium channels mostly in the hundreds to thousands but with a sodium Ki of 11.5 and an L-type calcium IC50 of 9.2 in frog myocytes, and GABA-A effects only at hundreds, with no binding seen at subanaesthetic doses in a human imaging study. The review itself places several targets within the clinically relevant range: nicotinic receptors (alpha4beta4 blocked at IC50 0.24 micromolar in oocytes, alpha3beta4 at 3.1, alpha7 at about 17 to 20, with the review calling concentrations up to about 10 micromolar clinically relevant), HCN1 channels (8.2 to 15.6 micromolar for the racemate, 4.1 to 7.4 for the S form, which it links to anaesthesia) and the muscarinic M1 value reported at 45 micromolar in cells and at 5.7 micromolar in oocytes, which it calls a clinically relevant concentration. The review states that many of these findings have not been confirmed by independent laboratories.

The metabolite account is preclinical as the review presents it: (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine is reported to produce antidepressant effects in rodents without the sensory dissociation, ataxia or abuse liability of ketamine in animal tests, and R-ketamine is reported to be a more potent and longer-lasting antidepressant than S-ketamine across rodent tests. The review states that no clinical study of R-ketamine in patients with depression had been published and that no clinical study had compared the two forms with each other or with the racemate, and it cites no human study in which a hydroxynorketamine was given. Six of the eleven authors are named as co-inventors on a patent application covering those metabolites, two of them also on a granted patent, and much of the supporting work comes from their own laboratories, including data marked unpublished.

On dopamine the review reports both sides: ketamine was described as a high-affinity D2 partial agonist (Ki 0.055 to 1.0 micromolar) and three human imaging studies reported reduced striatal D2 binding after subanaesthetic dosing, while two other human imaging studies found no change in striatal D2 availability, a human study found that a D2 blocker did not stop ketamine's psychosis-like effects, and one further study (Can et al., 2016) found no functional activity at any dopamine receptor subtype up to 10 micromolar, measured on human receptors expressed in cells, together with no change in electrically evoked dopamine release in mice.
